---
title: "Panel Balancedness"
---



## Definitions

As defined in the previous section, panel balancedness is evaluated separately within each *Current well-being* statistical series, with reference areas as the panel units and time periods as the repeated observations.

A panel is **strongly balanced** when every reference area is observed in every time period included in the panel's temporal support.

A panel is **weakly balanced** when all reference areas have the same number of observations, even if those observations do not occur in exactly the same time periods.

Strong balance implies weak balance under these definitions: if every reference area is observed in every time period, then every reference area necessarily has the same number of observations. Weak balance does not imply strong balance because reference areas may have the same number of observations in different time periods.

For reporting purposes, the statistical series are therefore classified into three mutually exclusive categories: **strongly balanced**, **weakly balanced**, and **unbalanced**. Series satisfying both balance definitions are classified as strongly balanced; the weakly balanced category contains only the remaining series that satisfy the weak-balance definition.

For each statistical series $k$, this project also reports the completion rate

$$
B_k =
\frac{N^{\mathrm{observed}}_k}
     {N^{\mathrm{units}}_k N^{\mathrm{periods}}_k},
$$

where $N^{\mathrm{observed}}_k$ is the number of observed reference area-period combinations, $N^{\mathrm{units}}_k$ is the number of reference areas, and $N^{\mathrm{periods}}_k$ is the number of time periods in the series. A value of $1$ indicates complete coverage of the corresponding reference area $\times$ time grid.

## Completion-rate distribution


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
panel_inventory |>
  ggplot2::ggplot(
    ggplot2::aes(x = completion_rate)
  ) +
  ggplot2::geom_histogram(
    bins = 30
  ) +
  ggplot2::labs(
    x = "Completion rate",
    y = "Number of statistical series"
  )
```

## Missingness with `panelView`

`panelView` is used here as a visual diagnostic rather than as the formal definition of balancedness [@mou2023panelview]. The explicit diagnostics above determine whether each statistical series is strongly or weakly balanced and quantify its completion rate. `panelView` complements those measures by showing where missing reference area-period observations occur.

For illustration, the figure below uses the statistical series with the highest completion rate among those spanning the maximum number of time periods. The table identifies the dimensions that define the selected series.




::: {#tbl-selected-series .cell tbl-cap='Dimensions defining the statistical series displayed below.'}

```{.r .cell-code}
series_definition |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    Dimension = dplyr::recode(
      DIMENSION,
      MEASURE = "Measure",
      UNIT_MEASURE = "Unit of measure",
      AGE = "Age",
      SEX = "Sex",
      EDUCATION_LEV = "Education level",
      DOMAIN = "Domain"
    ),
    `Selected value` = dplyr::coalesce(
      LABEL,
      "Label unavailable"
    )
  ) |>
  dplyr::select(
    Dimension,
    `Selected value`,
    `SDMX code` = CODE
  ) |>
  knitr::kable()
```

::: {.cell-output-display}


|Dimension       |Selected value      |SDMX code |
|:---------------|:-------------------|:---------|
|Measure         |Voter turnout       |8_2       |
|Unit of measure |Percentage of votes |PT_VOTES  |
|Age             |Total               |_T        |

|Education level |Total               |_T        |

```{.r .cell-code}
panelView::panelview(

  type = "missing",
  leave.gap = TRUE,
  axis.lab.angle = 45,
  xlab = "",
  ylab = ""
)
```
